irrational_computation.label: Irrational behaviour: consumer weakness at computation

stages.name: Government intervention: information provision (disadvantages)
stages.title: Information provision disadvantage
stages.sub: Why giving consumers information does not always change what they actually do.

steps.q: The government prints leaflets on the calories in fast food and posts them to every household. Will everyone actually read them?
steps.right: No, many people will bin them unread
steps.wrong: Yes, everyone reads what they are sent
steps.hint: Think about your own post: junk mail, letters, leaflets. Do you read all of it?

steps.q: A cigarette packet is covered in warnings, statistics and diagrams all at once. Does cramming in more facts make a smoker weigh them up more carefully?
steps.right: No, they may just tune it all out
steps.wrong: Yes, more facts always get processed more carefully
steps.hint: You already know consumers are weak at working through complicated numbers. What happens when there is a lot to work through at once?

steps.q: A tabloid headline and a peer-reviewed health study report the same statistic on sugar. Will a sceptical consumer treat both claims the same way?
steps.right: No, they may believe one and dismiss the other
steps.wrong: Yes, the same fact is believed regardless of where it comes from
steps.hint: Does it matter to you who is telling you something, not just what they are telling you?

steps.q: So even after the government pays to give consumers full, accurate information, will they necessarily end up making the choice that information was meant to produce?
steps.right: No, it may be ignored, overwhelming, distrusted or misread
steps.wrong: Yes, once given the facts they will act on them
steps.hint: Put together what happens when people skip leaflets, get swamped by detail, or doubt the source.
